Module 6›Chapter 1›The Power of Network Automation

The Power of Network Automation

Network automation is the process of automating the configuration, management, testing, deployment, and operation of physical and virtual network devices. It's a critical shift from manual, error-prone tasks to consistent, scalable, and efficient operations.

Reduced Errors

Eliminates human mistakes in configuration.

Ensured Consistency

Applies uniform configurations across devices.

Rapid Deployment

Accelerates service provisioning and changes.

Strategic Focus

Frees engineers for higher-value tasks.

Key Takeaway

Automation is essential for modern networks, enabling efficiency, consistency, and scalability while minimizing human error.

Manual vs. Automated Operations

Manual Configuration
  • Prone to human error
  • Time-consuming and slow
  • Difficult to scale across many devices
  • Inconsistent configurations
Automated Operations
  • Minimizes human error
  • Fast and efficient deployment
  • Highly scalable and repeatable
  • Ensures consistent network state

Real-world Connection

Imagine deploying 50 new branch offices. Manual configuration would take weeks and introduce errors. Automation can complete it in hours with perfect consistency.

screens.title: Junos OS Scripting: An Introduction
screens.narratorSegment: Junos OS is not just a powerful network operating system; it also provides a robust set of built-in automation features that allow you to extend its capabilities and integrate with external tools. At its core, Junos OS supports various types of scripts that can execute automatically based on specific triggers or on demand. Think of these scripts as specialized tools, each designed for a particular job within the network. We'll focus on three primary categories: operational scripts, commit scripts, and event scripts. Operational scripts are like custom commands you add to the Junos CLI, allowing you to perform complex tasks or gather specific data with a single input. Commit scripts are guardians of your configuration, automatically inspecting and validating changes before they become active, ensuring policy compliance. And event scripts are the network's reactive intelligence, triggering automated actions in response to specific system events like log messages or threshold breaches. Understanding these distinct mechanisms is the first step to effectively leveraging Junos OS for comprehensive network automation. Module 6›Chapter 1›Junos OS Scripting: An Introduction

Junos OS Scripting: An Introduction

Junos OS provides robust built-in automation features through various script types that execute based on triggers or on demand.

Operational (Op) Scripts

Extend the Junos CLI with custom commands for complex tasks or data gathering.

Commit Scripts

Enforce configuration policies and validate changes before they are committed.

Event Scripts

Trigger automated actions in response to specific system events or thresholds.

Key Takeaway

Junos OS provides three core script types—operational, commit, and event scripts—each serving a distinct purpose in automating network management and operations.

screens.title: Operational (Op) Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Operational scripts, often referred to as Op scripts, are a powerful way to extend the native Junos OS Command Line Interface, or CLI. Imagine needing to perform a complex series of commands or gather very specific data from multiple devices and then format it into a custom report. Instead of manually typing out each command every time, an Op script allows you to encapsulate all that logic into a single, easy-to-use custom CLI command. This significantly streamlines routine operational tasks and reduces the potential for errors that can occur with manual input. For example, you could create an Op script that, when executed, automatically collects interface statistics, checks BGP session states, and verifies routing table entries across several routing instances, presenting the consolidated information in a clear, custom format. These scripts are typically executed manually by an administrator directly from the Junos CLI using the op command, making them ideal for on-demand diagnostic checks, data collection, or custom reporting. They empower network engineers to tailor the CLI to their exact operational needs, enhancing efficiency and consistency in daily tasks. content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 1›Operational (Op) Scripts

Operational (Op) Scripts

Op scripts extend the Junos CLI, allowing administrators to create custom commands that perform complex tasks, gather specific data, or interact with external systems.

Key Purpose

Automate routine operational tasks and provide custom diagnostic or reporting tools directly from the CLI.

Execution Method

Manually invoked by an administrator using the op <script-name> command in the Junos CLI.

Key Takeaway

Op scripts are invaluable for customizing the Junos CLI, enabling efficient, on-demand execution of complex operational and data-gathering tasks.

Example: Custom Interface Report

Scenario

You need to quickly collect specific interface statistics (e.g., input/output errors) from multiple devices and present them in a custom, easy-to-read format.

Op Script Solution

An Op script can be written to query the device for these statistics, process the data, and then display it as a custom table or summary, all triggered by a single CLI command like op show-custom-interface-health.

Common Misconception

Op scripts are not for enforcing configuration policies; their primary role is for operational data gathering and custom command execution.

screens.title: Commit Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Commit scripts are incredibly powerful tools for maintaining the integrity and compliance of your network configuration. Unlike Op scripts, which are manually executed, commit scripts are automatically invoked whenever a user attempts to commit a configuration change to the Junos device. Their primary purpose is to act as a gatekeeper, enforcing configuration policies and validating changes before they are applied to the running configuration. A commit script can inspect the proposed configuration, compare it against predefined rules, and then take various actions: it can modify the configuration to ensure compliance, issue warnings, or even block the commit entirely if the proposed changes violate critical policies. For instance, you could write a commit script to ensure that all BGP peerings always use a specific authentication key, or that certain interfaces consistently have a particular firewall filter applied. This proactive validation significantly reduces the risk of introducing errors or non-compliant configurations into your live network. However, a common mistake is to create overly complex commit scripts that are difficult to debug or inadvertently block legitimate configurations. It's crucial to test commit scripts thoroughly in a lab environment before deploying them to production to avoid unintended operational disruptions.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 1›Commit Scripts

Commit Scripts

Commit scripts execute automatically during a configuration commit, enforcing policies, validating changes, or modifying the configuration to ensure compliance.

Key Purpose

Ensure configuration integrity and policy adherence by validating proposed changes before they become active.

Trigger & Actions

Invoked automatically on commit. Can inspect, modify, warn, or block the commit.

Key Takeaway

Commit scripts are essential for proactive configuration management, acting as a safeguard to prevent non-compliant or erroneous configurations from being applied.

Example: Enforcing BGP Authentication

Scenario

Your organization requires all BGP peerings to use a specific, strong authentication key for security reasons.

Commit Script Solution

A commit script can inspect the proposed BGP configuration. If a peering lacks the required authentication key, the script can block the commit and display an error message, preventing the insecure configuration from being applied.

Common Pitfall

Writing overly complex commit scripts can make them difficult to debug and may inadvertently block legitimate configuration changes, leading to operational delays.

screens.title: Event Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Event scripts are the reactive intelligence of Junos OS automation, designed to trigger automated actions in response to specific system events. Imagine a scenario where a critical log message indicates a hardware failure, or perhaps C P U utilization on your routing engine suddenly spikes above a predefined threshold. Instead of waiting for a human operator to detect and respond to these issues, an event script can be configured to automatically take action. These scripts are triggered by various system events, such as a log message matching a certain pattern, a threshold being exceeded, or even a hardware failure. Once triggered, an event script can perform a wide array of automated actions. This could include sending an email notification to the network operations center, collecting diagnostic data to aid in troubleshooting, or even attempting to self-heal the issue by restarting a process or reconfiguring an interface. For example, an event script could monitor for high C P U utilization and, if a threshold is crossed, automatically log relevant process information and send an alert. This reactive automation is crucial for maintaining network stability, reducing downtime, and ensuring a swift response to critical operational incidents, often before they impact services.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 1›Event Scripts

Event Scripts

Event scripts are triggered by specific system events (e.g., log messages, thresholds), performing automated actions in response to maintain network stability.

Key Purpose

Provide reactive automation to system changes, failures, or performance issues, minimizing human intervention.

Common Triggers

Log messages matching patterns, threshold exceedances (CPU, memory), hardware failures, interface state changes.

Key Takeaway

Event scripts enable Junos devices to autonomously respond to critical system events, enhancing network resilience and reducing downtime through automated actions.

Example: High CPU Utilization Alert

Scenario

The routing engine's CPU utilization on a critical device unexpectedly exceeds 90% for an extended period, indicating a potential issue.

Event Script Solution

An event script can monitor the CPU utilization. If the threshold is crossed, it can automatically log detailed process information, send an email alert to the NOC, and potentially even restart non-critical processes to alleviate the load.

Consideration

Poorly written event scripts can trigger false positives or execute unintended actions, potentially causing more disruption than the original event. Careful testing is vital.

screens.title: Choosing Your Language: SLAX or Python?
screens.narratorSegment: When it comes to scripting on Junos OS, you primarily have two powerful language options: SLAX and Python. Each has its unique strengths and is better suited for different types of tasks. SLAX, or Scripting Language for Junos OS, is an XML-based language specifically designed for manipulating Junos OS configuration and operational data. Since Junos OS inherently uses XML for its data structures, SLAX can be incredibly concise and efficient for tasks that involve directly parsing or modifying XML elements. It's often preferred for simpler, Junos-specific tasks where deep XML manipulation is required. On the other hand, Python has rapidly become the de facto language for network automation across the industry due to its versatility, extensive libraries, and broader applicability. For Junos, Python scripts often leverage the junos-eznc, or Junos PyEZ, library. This library provides a rich, object-oriented A P I for interacting with Junos devices via NETCONF, which we'll explore in a later chapter. Python is generally the preferred choice for more complex logic, integrating with external systems, or when you need to leverage existing Python libraries for tasks like data processing, A P I interactions, or advanced reporting. The key is to understand the nature of your automation task: for direct, XML-centric Junos operations, SLAX can be very effective, but for broader, more complex, and integrated automation, Python offers unparalleled flexibility and power.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 1›Choosing Your Language: SLAX or Python?

Choosing Your Language: SLAX or Python?

Junos OS supports scripting in two primary languages, each with distinct advantages for network automation tasks.

SLAX

Scripting Language for Junos OS (SLAX) is an XML-based language native to Junos, designed for manipulating its XML configuration and operational data.

  • XML-centric: Highly efficient for direct manipulation of Junos's XML data.
  • Native to Junos: Deep integration with Junos OS data models.
  • Concise for specific tasks: Ideal for simpler, Junos-specific XML parsing and modification.
  • Learning Curve: Can be steep if unfamiliar with XML/XSLT concepts.

Best Use Case

When deeply manipulating XML configuration or operational data within Junos.

Python

A versatile, general-purpose programming language with extensive libraries, widely adopted for network automation, leveraging Junos PyEZ.

  • Versatility: Broad applicability beyond Junos, extensive ecosystem.
  • Junos PyEZ: Rich API for interacting with Junos via NETCONF.
  • Complex Logic: Preferred for intricate logic, external system integration.

Module 6›Chapter 1›Building a Python Op Script: Interface Descriptions

Building a Python Op Script: Interface Descriptions

This script demonstrates how to create a custom operational command to display interface names and their configured descriptions using Python.

Script Purpose

Extend the Junos CLI to provide a quick overview of interface descriptions, aiding in documentation and troubleshooting.

Key Components

  • junos module for RPC interaction.
  • lxml for XML parsing and XPath.
  • Iterating through interface elements to extract data.
Key Takeaway

Python Op scripts, using Junos RPCs and XML parsing, enable powerful custom CLI commands for on-demand data retrieval and display.

show-interface-descriptions.py

# Example of a simple Junos Python op script to display interface descriptions
# Save this as /var/db/scripts/op/show-interface-descriptions.py

from junos import Junos_Configuration
from junos import Junos_RPC
from lxml import etree

def main():
    # Get the XML representation of the configuration
    with Junos_RPC() as rpc:
        response = rpc.get_config({'format': 'xml'})
        
        # Parse the XML response
        root = etree.fromstring(response.text)
        
        # Find all interfaces and their descriptions
        interfaces = root.xpath("//interfaces/interface")
        
        print("Interface Descriptions:")
        print("-----------------------")
        
        for interface in interfaces:
            name = interface.findtext("name")
            description = interface.findtext("description")
            
            if name:
                if description:
                    print(f"  {name}: {description}")
                else:
                    print(f"  {name}: (No Description)")
            
    print("-----------------------")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Configuration & Execution

set system scripts op file show-interface-descriptions.py
op show-interface-descriptions

Module 6›Chapter 1›Enforcing Policies with a Python Commit Script

Enforcing Policies with a Python Commit Script

This script demonstrates how to use a Python commit script to enforce a policy requiring all physical interfaces to have a description.

Script Purpose

Prevent configuration commits that violate the policy of requiring descriptions for physical interfaces, enhancing documentation and consistency.

Key Components

  • Junos_Configuration to access candidate config.
  • Junos_Commit.error() to block commits.
  • XPath to target specific interface types.
Key Takeaway

Python commit scripts are powerful for enforcing configuration policies, inspecting proposed changes, and blocking non-compliant commits to maintain network integrity.

check_interface_description.py

# check_interface_description.py
from junos import Junos_Configuration
from junos import Junos_Commit
from lxml import etree

def main():
    # Get the proposed configuration (candidate configuration)
    candidate_config = Junos_Configuration()
        
    # Find all physical interfaces in the proposed configuration
    interfaces_xpath = "//interfaces/interface[starts-with(name, 'ge-') or starts-with(name, 'xe-') or starts-with(name, 'et-')]"
        
    # Use XPath to find relevant interface elements
    physical_interfaces = candidate_config.xpath(interfaces_xpath)
        
    for interface_element in physical_interfaces:
        interface_name = interface_element.findtext("name")
        description_element = interface_element.find("description")
            
        # Check if the interface exists and if it lacks a description
        if interface_name and description_element is None:
            # If no description is found, reject the commit
            Junos_Commit.error(
                f"Commit failed: Interface '{interface_name}' must have a description."
            )
            # It's good practice to log the error as well
            Junos_Commit.log(
                f"Commit script 'check_interface_description.py' blocked commit for interface '{interface_name}' due to missing description."
            )
                
if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Configuration

set system scripts commit file check_interface_description.py

Unlike Op scripts, which are manually executed, commit scripts are automatically invoked whenever a user attempts to commit a configuration change to the Junos device. Their primary purpose is to act as a gatekeeper, enforcing configuration policies and validating changes before they are applied to the running configuration. A commit script can inspect the proposed configuration, compare it against predefined rules, and then take various actions: it can modify the configuration to ensure compliance, issue warnings, or even block the commit entirely if the proposed changes violate critical policies. For instance, you could write a commit script to ensure that all BGP peerings always use a specific authentication key, or that certain interfaces consistently have a particular firewall filter applied. These scripts are triggered by various system events, such as a log message matching a certain pattern, a threshold being exceeded, or even a hardware failure. Once triggered, an event script can perform a wide array of automated actions. This could include sending an email notification to the network operations center, collecting diagnostic data to aid in troubleshooting, or even attempting to self-heal the issue by restarting a process or reconfiguring an interface. For example, an event script could monitor for high C P U utilization and, if a threshold is crossed, automatically log relevant process information and send an alert. This reactive automation is crucial for maintaining network stability, reducing downtime, and ensuring a swift response to critical operational incidents, often before they impact services.
